To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the courts have been using a flawed analytical framework to evaluate intrabrand conduct.
the courts have been too quick to find anticompetitive agreements in the intraband market to be procompetitive.
the current state of antitrust law, which has been developed in response to interbrand market issues, is not well suited for dealing with intrabrand market issues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the antitrust treatment of intrabrand conduct.

the antitrust liability of a firm for engaging in intrabrand conduct that harms competition in the intraband market, while at the same time increasing competition in the interbrand market, or the market in which competing firms compete to sell to the ultimate consumer.
the question: What is the best way to protect competition within an intrabrand market?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the courts are not properly interpreting the Sherman Act to apply to intrabrand markets.
courts have been applying an interbrand analysis to intrabrand cases, and have thereby failed to protect intrabrand competition and the competitive marketplace as a whole.
courts should apply the rule of reason in intrabrand markets and should not apply the per se rule of the Sherman Act.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the current antitrust law regime, as it has developed over the years, is not well suited to address the problems in intrabrand markets and that the courts should be weaning themselves off of the interbrand addiction they have developed in order to give teeth to Sherman Act enforcement.
the antitrust laws should be interpreted in a way that allows for the prosecution of monopolies and anticompetitive practices in the intraband market.
the courts have been too willing to allow intrabrand anticompetitive behavior to occur.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the courts should not allow the intrabrand distributor's anticompetitive behavior to be excused on the grounds that it will increase interbrand competition.
courts should not rely on the interbrand efficiency of a market as a justification for the exclusion of intrabrand competitors.
courts are currently applying a flawed legal standard to determine whether a vertical nonprice agreement violates section 1 of the Sherman Act.
